facts.claim: "Hang in There" is on Stephen Wilson Jr.'s debut double album søn of dad, released September 15, 2023 on Big Loud Records.
Big Loud's official tracklist lists "Hang in There" as track 12 and credits Stephen Wilson Jr. as the sole writer.
The track runs about 3 minutes 52 seconds.
Audiomack's listing for the deluxe-edition version of the song credits Ben West as producer.

Discogs credits the søn of dad album as produced and programmed by Ben West and Stephen Wilson Jr., with Billy Justineau on pump organ. The album was recorded at Farmland Studios, Whistle Stop, Stone Airplane and Aashrum Studios, and mastered at Infrasonic Sound in Nashville.
Saving Country Music says "Hang In There" was inspired by a personal memento owned by Wilson's father.
søn of dad is a 22-song tribute to Wilson's late father. It was released on the fifth anniversary of his death.
Wilson's father, Stephen Wilson Sr., died on September 15, 2018 after emergency surgery.
Wilson says he began keeping a record of what he was going through after his father died. He describes the songs on søn of dad as gifts that helped him understand that experience.

Before his solo career, Wilson was an Indiana Golden Gloves boxing finalist, a microbiologist and scientist, an indie-rock guitarist and a BMG-signed Nashville songwriter. His songs were cut by Old Dominion, Tim McGraw and Caitlyn Smith, among others.

research.lineage: Wilson describes his sound as "Death Cab for Country", a Nashville country-rock and Americana blend that draws on indie rock and grunge, and he is signed to the country label Big Loud.

draft:
The father in **Hang in There** gets the best line, and he gets it from the passenger seat: "boy would ya go a little slower? / You're worrisome son, make your old man look a little older." It's a dad joke with a worry folded inside it, the kind of thing a parent says to a grown kid so the fear comes out as teasing. Stephen Wilson Jr. puts it right after the flattest sentence in the song, "It's not right he's not here," and the pairing does the work. Grief arrives as a complaint. Then memory answers with a voice that's still alive, still needling.

The song sits on Wilson's debut double album *søn of dad*, a 22-song tribute to his father, Stephen Wilson Sr., who died in September 2018 after emergency surgery. The record came out on the fifth anniversary of that death. Wilson wrote this one alone, and it grew out of a memento of his father's. In the lyric it's a beaded necklace from a spring trip to Jamaica, and the narrator is honest about how it looks from outside: "to most it ain't worth nothin'." That line is the song's quiet defense of private value. The beads aren't proof of anything. They're the one thing he gets to keep.

The chorus turns the title into a pun and a plea at once. The necklace hangs from the rearview mirror, so the father rides along again, swapped from the passenger seat into the corner of the son's eye. "Hang in there" is also what you say to someone who's struggling, and the narrator says it to himself by way of a dead man's souvenir. The song admits it's "more like a prayer." Then comes the stranger line, "an empty page to write a better ending." Whose ending isn't clear. It could be the father's, cut short, or the son's own. The song lets both stay open, and that unease sits under the comfort.

The sound stays close. A fingerpicked acoustic guitar carries its own bass line under arpeggiated chords, slide guitar draws long notes behind it, and the tempo sways slowly. Wilson sings low and a little raspy, warm and conversational, with no harmonies to soften it. The room sounds small and dry, as if he's talking from the driver's seat. It's a long way from the indie-rock and grunge edges he folds into the "Death Cab for Country" blend he calls his sound. Here it's a plain country-folk ballad, and the plainness fits. The chorus repeats more than it needs to near the end, and "call it precious" reads like a placeholder. But the repetition works like a mantra.

The song sticks because it shows you how grief really travels: hanging from the mirror, swinging every time you take a turn too fast.
